patients.summary: Librarian in her thirties with type 1 von Willebrand disease, Kallmann syndrome on hormone replacement, and chronic iron deficiency, who conceives twice through ovulation induction. Her first vaginal birth in 2023 brings a uterine inversion, two hemorrhages and a D&C; a 2025 cesarean bleeds again. The low cortisol and free T4 flagged in 2023 go unpursued until endocrinology names postpartum hypopituitarism in June 2026.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

Ms. Klein is a 31-year-old librarian moving her care here; her old office was an hour's drive and she wanted one closer to home in Goshen. She and her husband would like to start a family this year and she already has a reproductive endocrinology consult on the calendar for next month.

HISTORY
- Von Willebrand disease, type 1. Bruised easily and had a lot of nosebleeds as a child; worked up and diagnosed around age 13. Follows with a hematologist who prescribes nasal desmopressin. She uses it a few times a year for nosebleeds that won't stop. Never needed a transfusion.
- Kallmann syndrome. No puberty by 17 and has never been able to smell much; diagnosed then with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Has been on continuous estrogen-progestin replacement since. Understands she will need ovulation induction to conceive.
- Iron deficiency anemia for years, on ferrous sulfate daily. Tolerates it with some constipation.
- Surgical: none.

MEDICATIONS: ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily; desmopressin nasal 150 mcg PRN bleeding; ethinyl estradiol 5 mcg / norethindrone acetate 1 mg one tab daily; vitamin D3 2000 IU daily.
ALLERGIES: latex causes a contact rash. No drug allergies.

FAMILY HISTORY: Mother has type 1 vWD too, with heavy periods that ended in a hysterectomy at 42. Father went through puberty late (about 16) and has a poor sense of smell; his doctors thought he probably carries a milder form of the same condition. One sister has primary infertility and lost her periods.

SOCIAL: Married. Works at a public library. Never smoked, does not drink.

ROS: Energy fair. Occasional nosebleeds. No melena. Otherwise negative.

EXAM: Thin, well appearing. Vitals as recorded. HEENT unremarkable. Neck supple, thyroid not enlarged. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. Skin: a couple of small bruises on the shins, no petechiae. Neuro grossly intact.

ASSESSMENT / PLAN
1. Iron deficiency anemia, chronic - CBC, iron studies today. Continue iron.
2. vWD type 1 - stable. Will need a delivery plan with obstetrics and her hematologist once pregnant. Requesting hematology records.
3. Kallmann syndrome / infertility - REI consult next month. Continue hormone replacement until they say otherwise.
4. Health maintenance - CMP, TSH, lipids, vitamin D; HIV and hep C screening once, she agrees. Pap last year at old practice, normal per patient; records requested. PHQ-2 0.

Return after the REI visit or sooner as needed.

documents.title: Your recent labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Maya, your labs are back. Hemoglobin is 11.4, a little low, and your ferritin (iron stores) is 9, which is low - consistent with the iron deficiency you've had for years. Please keep taking the iron every day; taking it with a little orange juice and away from tea or coffee helps it absorb. Kidney, liver, thyroid, cholesterol and vitamin D are all fine, and the HIV and hepatitis C screens are negative. Good luck at your REI appointment.

documents.title: Hematology Summary Letter
documents.author: hematology
documents.body:
Outside hematology - summary for new primary care physician

This 31-year-old woman has been followed here for type 1 von Willebrand disease since her early teens. Her bleeding history has been mucocutaneous: easy bruising and recurrent epistaxis. She responds to desmopressin and keeps an intranasal spray at home for nosebleeds that do not settle with pressure. She has not needed factor concentrate or transfusion.

She has told us she plans a pregnancy through reproductive endocrinology. When she is pregnant, her obstetric team should contact us so a delivery plan can be made. Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin. Latex allergy noted.

Please contact our office with questions.

documents.title: Reproductive Endocrinology Consultation
documents.author: reproductive endocrinology
documents.body:
REPRODUCTIVE ENDOCRINOLOGY - NEW CONSULTATION
Date of visit: 2022-06-21

Reason: desires conception; known Kallmann syndrome.

Ms. Klein, 31, has isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia, diagnosed at 17, maintained on continuous ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone. She has never ovulated spontaneously. Her husband's evaluation is pending. Type 1 von Willebrand disease is followed by hematology. Iron deficiency on oral iron. Latex allergy - our procedure rooms are latex-free.

Impression: hypogonadotropic infertility, a good candidate for gonadotropin ovulation induction.

Plan:
- Gonadotropin ovulation induction with ultrasound and estradiol monitoring here, then an hCG trigger.
- Stop the hormone replacement once we schedule the first stimulation cycle; we will tell her when.
- We will keep her primary care physician updated.

documents.body: Hi - just wanted you to know the REI office called today and my blood test is positive! We're over the moon. They'll do an ultrasound in a couple of weeks. Is there anything I should stop taking? I'm on iron and vitamin D. Also do I still get a flu shot?

documents.title: RE: Good news
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Congratulations to you both! Keep the iron and vitamin D. Use the desmopressin only if you have a bleed that won't stop, and let us or your OB know if you do. Yes - the flu shot is recommended in pregnancy and so is the updated COVID booster. The nurse can give both; the front desk will reach out to schedule.

OUTSIDE OBSTETRICS - PRENATAL UPDATE TO PRIMARY CARE
Date of visit: 2023-02-24

G1 at 20 weeks by early ultrasound dating, conceived with ovulation induction. Doing well.

Anatomy ultrasound today: single live intrauterine fetus, growth appropriate for gestational age, anatomy survey complete and normal. Placenta posterior and well clear of the cervix. Amniotic fluid normal.

History reviewed: type 1 von Willebrand disease (hematology aware of the pregnancy), Kallmann syndrome, iron deficiency on oral iron. Latex allergy flagged on her chart and on the labor unit.

Plan: routine prenatal visits; no further ultrasound planned unless there is a clinical question. Delivery at our hospital's labor unit with hematology available.

documents.title: Obstetric Discharge Summary
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OBSTETRIC DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 2023-07-01  Discharged: 2023-07-03

Patient: 32-year-old G1, term, conceived with ovulation induction. Type 1 von Willebrand disease, Kallmann syndrome, chronic iron deficiency on oral iron. Latex allergy (contact dermatitis); no drug allergies.

COURSE
Presented in spontaneous labor. Labor progressed on its own with no induction, augmentation or instruments. At 03:40 she had a vaginal delivery of a healthy boy. Oxytocin was given for the third stage only. The placenta delivered a few minutes later; on inspection its margin was irregular and a vessel coursed out onto the membranes.

Within about half an hour she was bleeding heavily. Pressure fell to 80/50 with a heart rate of 120; she became agitated and confused, and her skin was cool and clammy. The fundus could not be felt abdominally and a large, red, rounded mass was protruding from the vagina - acute uterine inversion. Hemoglobin had been 12 on admission and was 9 at that point; platelets 250, INR 1.1. Type A positive.

She was taken to the operating room and the uterus was manually replaced under anesthesia. Her pressure reached a low of 80/40 during the reduction, and she received 4 units of packed red cells. After replacement the uterus was firm and of expected postpartum size, with no vaginal or cervical lacerations, but bleeding persisted despite oxytocin and did not respond to fundal massage. Afebrile, BP 92/60, HR 122; hemoglobin 7.4. Given her von Willebrand disease, intravenous desmopressin was given on hematology's advice and the bleeding settled over the next hour.

She recovered on the postpartum unit, ambulating and tolerating diet. Breastfeeding was started with lactation support.

DIAGNOSES: vaginal delivery at term; acute uterine inversion, manually reduced; acute postpartum hemorrhage with hypovolemic shock; acute blood-loss anemia, transfused; type 1 von Willebrand disease.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS: ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily; vitamin D3 2000 IU daily; desmopressin nasal spray as needed for bleeding.

FOLLOW-UP: obstetrics postpartum visit; primary care in 1-2 weeks for anemia. Return for heavy bleeding, fever or dizziness.

reports.text: Transabdominal and transvaginal views. Postpartum uterus, enlarged as expected for day 3 after vaginal delivery, normal in orientation. Endometrial cavity contains a small amount of fluid; no echogenic mass and no internal vascularity to suggest retained placental tissue. Ovaries unremarkable. No free fluid.
reports.conclusion: No sonographic evidence of retained products of conception.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD
Date of service: 2023-07-04

CC: postpartum bleeding.

HPI: 32F, day 3 after a vaginal delivery complicated by uterine inversion and hemorrhage (discharged from our L&D yesterday). Bleeding has been steady since she got home and heavier through the night; her husband says she has been soaking pads. Has type 1 vWD and chronic iron deficiency. Bruises easily and has had frequent nosebleeds all her life; says her mother bleeds the same way.
Allergies: latex (rash). No drug allergies.
Meds: ferrous sulfate, vitamin D3, desmopressin nasal PRN.

EXAM on arrival: BP 110/70, HR 98, afebrile. Pale. Uterus firm on palpation. Steady vaginal bleeding.
Labs: Hgb 9.2, plt 250, PT 12, aPTT 38 (mildly prolonged), fibrinogen normal.
Pelvic US: no retained tissue seen.
Given IV desmopressin per hematology by phone; IV fluids; OB called.

At 09:10 she developed severe crampy abdominal pain and felt faint. Pale and diaphoretic. BP 90/60, HR 120. Speculum: cervix dilated with a firm, rounded mass of tissue sitting in the os. Repeat labs Hgb 8, Hct 24%, plt 250, PT 12, PTT 30.

IMPRESSION: secondary postpartum hemorrhage, likely retained tissue despite the ultrasound; vWD.
DISPOSITION: to the OR with OB for evacuation, then admission to obstetrics.

conditions.label: Secondary postpartum hemorrhage due to retained products of conception

reports.text: Specimen: uterine contents, dilation and curettage. Gross: multiple fragments of red-tan soft tissue and blood clot, 4.0 x 3.0 x 1.0 cm in aggregate. Microscopic: chorionic villi and decidua admixed with blood clot.

documents.title: Readmission Discharge Summary
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OBSTETRIC READMISSION - DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 2023-07-04  Discharged: 2023-07-09

Reason: secondary postpartum hemorrhage, postpartum day 3.

She came back through our ED with ongoing bleeding (see ED record). Ultrasound had not shown retained tissue, but on exam there was tissue at a dilated os and she was becoming unstable. Suction dilation and curettage was done the morning of 07/04 with a moderate amount of placental tissue removed; bleeding stopped promptly afterward. Pathology confirmed placental tissue.

On 07/08, one week out from delivery, medicine was asked to see her for fatigue (see consult). Pressures ran soft but she stayed stable. Breastfeeding has been hard - very little milk despite frequent feeds; lactation saw her twice and she is supplementing with formula.

DIAGNOSES: secondary postpartum hemorrhage due to retained products of conception, s/p D&C; recent uterine inversion and primary PPH (07/01); acute blood-loss anemia; type 1 von Willebrand disease; Kallmann syndrome; chronic iron deficiency.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS: unchanged - ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily, vitamin D3, desmopressin nasal PRN.

FOLLOW-UP: obstetrics postpartum visit; primary care within 2 weeks.

documents.title: Internal Medicine Inpatient Consultation
documents.author: internal medicine
documents.body:
INTERNAL MEDICINE CONSULTATION
Date: 2023-07-08
Requested by obstetrics for fatigue.

She is a week out from the birth of her son. The delivery was followed by a uterine inversion reduced in the OR (pressure down to 80/40 there, 4 units PRBC) and on day 3 a second bleed needing D&C. Since then she has felt more and more worn out, struggles to manage the baby's care, and her milk supply is poor even though she is putting him to the breast often. Background: type 1 vWD, Kallmann syndrome, iron deficiency.

Exam: pale, pressures mildly low, alert. No fever. Abdomen soft, uterus firm and nontender. No signs of infection.

Impression: postpartum fatigue, most likely from heavy blood loss on top of chronic iron deficiency and the demands of a newborn.
Recommendations: continue oral iron; primary care follow-up within 2 weeks with a CBC; return for worsening dizziness or bleeding.

documents.title: Hospital Records Received
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Received from the hospital: two discharge summaries (07/01-07/03 and 07/04-07/09), ED record 07/04, pathology. Indexed and routed to PCP. Pt's husband called asking for a post-hospital appointment; RN to call.

documents.title: Post-discharge call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called pt 3 days after discharge. Bleeding now light, no clots. No fever. Very tired; a bit dizzy getting out of bed, careful on the stairs. Baby doing well; mostly formula now. Taking iron. Reviewed reasons to go back to the ED (soaking a pad an hour, fainting, fever). Video visit booked with PCP for next week, CBC to follow.

documents.title: Telehealth Visit - Post-Hospital
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit; she is at home with the baby asleep beside her. Identity confirmed.

Two hospital stays after her son's birth on 7/1: uterine inversion manually reduced with PPH and 4 units PRBC, then day-3 readmission for secondary PPH with retained placenta, D&C on 7/4. Discharge summaries and pathology reviewed.

Now 18 days postpartum. Bleeding light. Exhausted, short of breath on the stairs, lightheaded when she first stands. Milk never really came in; the baby is on formula and she has stopped trying to pump. Appetite poor. Mood: tearful at times, but says it's mostly fatigue; no thoughts of harming herself or the baby. Husband home on leave for another week.

Meds: ferrous sulfate daily, vitamin D3, desmopressin nasal PRN (has not needed it at home). Hormone replacement still off since the induction cycles.

A/P:
- Acute blood-loss anemia on chronic iron deficiency: CBC tomorrow. Continue iron. Discussed IV iron if no recovery.
- Postpartum, s/p uterine inversion and secondary PPH: OB visit scheduled.
- Hormone replacement: will revisit at the 6-week mark since she is not breastfeeding.
- In-person visit at 6 weeks postpartum. Sooner if dizziness worsens.

documents.title: CBC result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hgb 8.7, up from the hospital nadir. Platelets fine. Message sent: recovering slowly; keep iron daily; see me at 6 weeks.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
OFFICE VISIT - 6 weeks postpartum

First slot of the day so we could draw fasting morning labs.

S: Six weeks after a vaginal delivery complicated by uterine inversion with major hemorrhage (4 u PRBC) and a day-3 secondary PPH with D&C. Still bone-tired; naps whenever the baby does and wakes unrefreshed. Never got a real milk supply and gave up nursing; baby thriving on formula. Gets woozy when she stands up quickly, has had to sit on the floor twice. Not hungry; eats because she should. Lochia finished. No fevers. No headaches or vision change.

Meds: ferrous sulfate 325 daily, vitamin D3, desmopressin nasal PRN (unused). HRT off since last summer's induction cycles.

O: BP 90/60, HR 55. Pale, skin a little dry. Conjunctivae pale. Heart regular, slow, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, uterus not palpable. No edema. PHQ-9 5, no self-harm thoughts.

A/P:
1. Postpartum fatigue with orthostatic dizziness and failed lactation after severe hemorrhage. Anemia is part of it, but the poor milk supply and low pressure after a bleed this size make me want to look at the pituitary too. Drawing BMP, morning cortisol, TSH and free T4, prolactin, CBC and ferritin.
2. Acute blood-loss anemia on iron deficiency - continue iron, recheck counts today.
3. Kallmann syndrome - not breastfeeding and six weeks out, so restarting her estradiol/norethindrone today.
4. Fluids and salt liberally; rise slowly.
Will call with results.

orders.reason: Low morning cortisol and low free T4 after postpartum hemorrhage

documents.title: Results - 8/14 labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Na 130, K 5.2. AM cortisol 3. TSH 0.5 with free T4 0.7 (low). Prolactin 5. Hgb 10.3, ferritin 11.

Sodium low and cortisol and free T4 both low with a TSH that isn't elevated - in the setting of her hemorrhage this needs endocrinology. Referral placed, asked for a soon appointment. Repeat AM cortisol and BMP in 1-2 weeks. Hgb improving.

Spoke with pt by phone, explained results and that endocrinology will evaluate her pituitary function. She has the referral number.

documents.title: Cancelled specialist appointment
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Pt called: endocrinology appointment for 9/14 - she cancelled it. Baby has had a rough week and she can't make the drive. Says she's feeling a little better. Will call them to rebook. Reminded her the repeat lab order is in for her to get drawn here.

Says she is tired but less than in the summer - the baby sleeps longer stretches now. Back at the library part-time since October. Lightheadedness only now and then. Eating better. Back on her estradiol/norethindrone. No nosebleeds lately.

She never rebooked endocrinology; encouraged her again and gave her the number.

Exam: BP and pulse as recorded. Pale-ish but better color. Heart and lungs normal. PHQ-9 3.

- Iron deficiency anemia - CBC and ferritin today, continue iron.
- Postpartum hemorrhage, inversion, retained placenta - resolved; cleaning up problem list.
- Kallmann syndrome - continue HRT.
RTC spring for a physical.

documents.title: Refill - nose spray

documents.body: Could you send a refill of my desmopressin spray? My hematologist retired and the bottle I have expired in January. I've only used it twice this winter for nosebleeds.

documents.title: RE: Refill - nose spray
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Sent a new bottle to your pharmacy. Same as before: one spray in one nostril only for a bleed that won't stop with 10-15 minutes of pressure, and no more than one dose in a day without calling. Limit how much water you drink for the rest of that day. If you'd like a new hematologist, let us know and we'll set it up.

reports.text: Specimen: liquid-based cervical cytology. Specimen adequacy: satisfactory for evaluation; transformation zone component present. Interpretation: negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. High-risk HPV: not detected.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ANNUAL PHYSICAL

33 y/o, son is 10 months old and walking along the furniture. Working full time at the library again. Energy 'fine for a parent of a baby.' Occasional nosebleed. On HRT, no breakthrough bleeding. No new concerns.

Meds: ferrous sulfate 325 daily, ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone acetate 5 mcg/1 mg daily, vitamin D3 2000 IU, desmopressin nasal PRN.
Allergies: latex.
PMH: vWD type 1, Kallmann syndrome, iron deficiency; 2023 delivery with uterine inversion, PPH x2, D&C.
FH/SH unchanged. Never smoker, no alcohol.

ROS otherwise negative.

EXAM: Slim, well. Vitals as recorded. HEENT normal, no epistaxis. Thyroid normal. Heart RRR without murmur; lungs clear. Breasts deferred - pt declined today. Abdomen benign. Pelvic: external genitalia normal, cervix normal; Pap/HPV obtained (non-latex speculum cover and gloves). Skin: no bruising today. Mood bright, PHQ-2 0.

PLAN:
- CBC, ferritin, lipids, vitamin D.
- Pap with HPV today.
- Continue meds. Flu and COVID in the fall.
- Hematology: her doctor has retired; she'll think about a new one before any future pregnancy.

documents.title: Physical results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Maya, your Pap is normal and HPV negative, so the next one isn't due for five years. Hemoglobin 11.7 and ferritin 21 - the best they've been since you joined us. Cholesterol is good and vitamin D is 34. Keep the iron going.

documents.title: Telehealth Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit from the library break room; identity confirmed.

She and her husband want a second child and she has asked the same REI group to see her again in January. Wants to know what to tell them and whether anything should change first.

Discussed: last pregnancy ended with inversion and two hemorrhages; obstetrics and REI should know that from the start, and a hematologist should be involved in delivery planning. No symptoms today. Continue current meds. Will send her a summary of the 2023 hospital stays through the portal so she can share it.

documents.title: Obstetrics Prenatal Update
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OUTSIDE OBSTETRICS - LETTER TO PRIMARY CARE
Date of visit: 2025-08-19

G2P1 at about 22 weeks, conceived with ovulation induction. Anatomy ultrasound normal: appropriately grown single fetus, normal survey, placenta fundal and clear of the os.

History: her first birth (2023) was vaginal and was followed by an acute uterine inversion with primary postpartum hemorrhage needing manual replacement and transfusion, then a secondary hemorrhage from retained placenta needing D&C. Type 1 von Willebrand disease. Kallmann syndrome. Iron deficiency.

Plan after counseling: scheduled cesarean at 39 weeks given the prior inversion, with hematology input on hemostatic support. She has asked for tubal ligation at the same operation and has signed consent. Blood bank sample and crossmatch to be arranged before surgery.

OBSTETRIC DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 2025-12-16  Discharged: 2025-12-19

34-year-old G2P1 at 39 weeks for scheduled cesarean (indication: prior acute uterine inversion) and bilateral tubal ligation. Type 1 von Willebrand disease - hematology recommendations followed in the OR. Kallmann syndrome. Iron deficiency. Latex allergy - latex-free room.

PROCEDURE 12/16: low transverse cesarean section under spinal anesthesia with delivery of a healthy infant, followed by bilateral tubal ligation. The case was complicated by significant hemorrhage; she was transfused 2 units of packed red cells and hemostasis was achieved.

Postoperative course: slow to mobilize because of fatigue and lightheadedness, otherwise unremarkable. Incision clean. Breastfeeding attempted with lactation support; supply low, supplementing.

DIAGNOSES: term pregnancy, delivered by cesarean; bilateral tubal ligation; postpartum hemorrhage with acute blood-loss anemia, transfused; type 1 von Willebrand disease.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS: ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily; vitamin D3 2000 IU daily; desmopressin nasal PRN.

FOLLOW-UP: obstetrics wound check in one week.

documents.title: Obstetrics Post-operative Visit
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OBSTETRICS - POSTOPERATIVE VISIT
Date of visit: 2025-12-22

One week after her cesarean and tubal ligation (second child), a delivery complicated by hemorrhage requiring transfusion. She came with her husband and the baby.

She describes deep exhaustion, an inability to produce any milk though she has been putting the baby to the breast often, lightheadedness whenever she stands, and difficulty keeping her mind on things. Of note she has had no vaginal bleeding or lochia at all since the delivery.

Vitals: BP 92/56, pulse 92. Exam unremarkable other than pallor; incision healing well.
Labs today: sodium 132, glucose 64. Urine pregnancy test negative.

Assessment: postoperative check after cesarean with significant hemorrhage. Her symptoms, absent lochia, low sodium and low glucose after a second major postpartum bleed raise concern for pituitary insufficiency.
Plan: we are sending this note to her primary care physician and recommend prompt endocrinology evaluation of pituitary function. Return precautions given for vomiting, confusion or fainting.

documents.title: Endocrinology Consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
ENDOCRINOLOGY - CONSULTATION LETTER
Date of visit: 2026-06-23
Referred by: primary care

Dear colleague,

I saw Ms. Klein, 35, whom our group last followed years ago for her Kallmann syndrome. She delivered her second child by cesarean six months ago; that delivery was complicated by hemorrhage and transfusion, as was her first in 2023 (uterine inversion, then retained placenta). Since December she has not had a period and never produced milk. She is tired all the time and has noticed thinning of her pubic and axillary hair. Her estradiol/norethindrone has been off since January 2025 for fertility treatment.

Other history: type 1 von Willebrand disease; iron deficiency anemia; tubal ligation at the cesarean. Medications: ferrous sulfate, vitamin D3, desmopressin nasal as needed. Allergy: latex.

Exam: BP 90/60. BMI 19. Pale. No galactorrhea on breast exam.

Labs this morning (08:05): sodium 130, potassium 5.2, calcium 9.0; cortisol 3 mcg/dL; TSH 0.5 with free T4 0.8; prolactin 5.

Assessment: hypopituitarism following postpartum hemorrhage (Sheehan syndrome), with secondary adrenal insufficiency and central hypothyroidism. Low prolactin explains the failed lactation. The underlying Kallmann syndrome means her gonadotropin deficiency predates this.

Plan:
1. Hydrocortisone 10 mg on waking and 5 mg at about 2 PM, started today. Sick-day rules reviewed: double the doses for fever or illness, and seek care for vomiting. A medical alert ID and an emergency steroid letter given.
2. Levothyroxine 50 mcg daily, starting four days after the hydrocortisone. Dose by free T4, not TSH.
3. Resume ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone acetate 5 mcg/1 mg daily for estrogen replacement.
4. Desmopressin only for bleeding; with her low sodium, limit fluids that day.
5. Labs and visit here in 6 weeks.

Thank you for the referral.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/u after endocrinology (letter 6/23 reviewed).

S: Endocrinology diagnosed postpartum hypopituitarism - Sheehan's - with secondary adrenal insufficiency and central hypothyroidism. Started hydrocortisone 10 mg on waking / 5 mg early afternoon on 6/23; levothyroxine 50 mcg began 6/27; back on her estradiol/norethindrone. After a week she already feels steadier on her feet and a bit less flat in the afternoons. No vomiting, no fevers. Has her alert bracelet ordered and the emergency letter in her bag.

Meds: hydrocortisone 10 mg AM / 5 mg PM, levothyroxine 50 mcg daily, ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone acetate 5 mcg/1 mg daily, ferrous sulfate 325 daily, vitamin D3 2000 IU, desmopressin nasal PRN.

O: BP 94/62. Weight 51.7 kg. Thin, pale. Heart regular, lungs clear. No edema. PHQ-2 1.

A/P:
1. Hypopituitarism after postpartum hemorrhage - added to problem list; replacement per endocrinology. Reviewed sick-day doubling and when to go to the ED. Flagged chart: stress-dose steroids for any procedure or acute illness.
2. Hyponatremia - expect improvement on hydrocortisone; endocrinology rechecks in 6 weeks.
3. Kallmann syndrome - HRT resumed.
4. Iron deficiency - continue iron.
5. vWD - desmopressin sparingly, fluids limited that day.
RTC September.

documents.author: patient
documents.body: Just a note - two weeks on the hydrocortisone and I'm noticeably better. I took the stairs at work today without having to stop. My husband says I'm talking more. The bracelet came. Thank you.

documents.title: RE: Two weeks in
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: That is so good to hear. Keep everything as endocrinology set it, and remember to double the hydrocortisone if you get sick. See you in September.
